P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: No. As an EU member state, Slovenia applies Article 63 TFEU, which prohibits restrictions on capital movements and payments between EU countries and with non-EU countries. Banks still apply AML/KYC checks and may ask for the source of funds.

sources.title: Free movement of capital (European Parliament Fact Sheet)
sources.quote: Article 63 TFEU prohibits all restrictions on the movement of capital and payments between EU countries, as well as between EU and non-EU countries.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Very likely yes: Article 63 TFEU removes capital-movement restrictions, and EU banks and e-money institutions commonly offer foreign-currency or multi-currency accounts. No Slovenia-specific source on account rules was captured.
P2_fcy_account.note: Only the general EU capital-movement source captured; no national bank/regulator source on FCY accounts (2026-10-23).

sources.title: Free movement of capital (European Parliament Fact Sheet)
sources.quote: ensuring that payments in relation to those capital movements can be executed without restrictions, so that individuals and businesses can use, invest and/or save their money or financial assets anywhere within the EU as well as in non-EU countries.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: A sole trader (samostojni podjetnik, s.p.) registers in the Slovenian Business Register (Poslovni register Slovenije) through the SPOT portal online or at a SPOT point (AJPES branches); not at a notary. Registration for compulsory social insurance (form M-1, ZZZS) is also handled via SPOT. Fees not captured.

L2_tax_id.question: Tax ID: who needs one, how to get it?
L2_tax_id.answer: Official TIN description supplied by Slovenia to the OECD: "The SI tax number (TIN) is the identification sign, which defines the taxpayer (individuals and legal entities). It is used for uniform specification and connection of data in the taxpayer’s tax records, which are managed by the Financial Administration. The TIN is used for all taxes. However , the SI TIN is not reported on official documents of identification (like passport, identity card)." How a freelancer applies (forms, online portal, fees) was not captured.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Tax residents of Slovenia are taxed on worldwide income (see quoted rules for exceptions such as remittance-basis regimes). Five brackets from 16% (2026). Inference (general source principle, not quoted): work performed while living in Slovenia for foreign clients is normally taxable in Slovenia.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: National threshold: EUR 60,000 of annual taxable turnover (raised from EUR 50,000 from 1 January 2025) for Slovenian-established businesses. It does not apply to foreign taxable persons. The standard VAT rate is 22%. Under the EU SME scheme, small businesses below a national threshold (at most EUR 85,000) can be exempt on domestic sales. Where services are taxed (EU-wide rules, illustrated by Irish Revenue guidance): (1) B2B, meaning services to business customers in other EU countries or outside the EU, are taxed where the customer is established, so no Slovenia VAT is charged; EU business customers self-account under the reverse charge. (2) B2C services to private individuals are, as a rule, taxed where the supplier is established, so Slovenia VAT applies once you are VAT-registered. (3) Exception: consultancy, legal, accounting, engineering, data-processing, advertising, licensing and electronically supplied services to private customers outside the EU are outside EU VAT, subject to 'use and enjoyment' rules. Electronically supplied services to private customers in other EU countries follow special OSS rules (not captured here).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies directly in Slovenia, supervised by the national data protection authority. It covers EU businesses and non-EU businesses offering goods or services to people in the EU.

sources.title: Data protection (European Commission)
sources.quote: EU data protection legislation is comprised of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Data Protection Regulation for EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies (EUDPR).

sources.title: Data protection and online privacy (Your Europe)
sources.quote: These rules apply to both companies and organisations (public and private) in the EU and those based outside the EU who offer goods or services in the EU , such as Facebook or Amazon, whenever these companies request or re-use the personal data of individuals in the EU.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: EU consumer law gives a 14-day withdrawal right for online and distance purchases without justification: 14 days from delivery for goods, and from conclusion of the contract for services. Exceptions include personalised goods, perishables and date-specific services.

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: This means you can cancel the contract within 14 days without providing any justification (the "cooling-off period").

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: For goods this means 14 days from the date of delivery, for services 14 days after the day the contract was agreed.

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: Flat-rate expenses (normirani s.p.): tax is computed on revenue minus deemed expenses, with no actual-expense bookkeeping. FURS's 2026 worked example (full-time s.p.) allows 80% deemed expenses on revenue up to EUR 60,000 and 0% above. From 2026 the tax is progressive. Full-time self-employed (compulsorily insured at least 9 months continuously): 20% of the tax base up to EUR 72,000, 35% above. Others: 20% up to EUR 33,000, 35% above. Entry for 2026 required 2025 revenue at most EUR 50,000, or EUR 120,000 if full-time insured. You must leave if average revenue over the two previous years exceeds EUR 120,000, EUR 85,000 or EUR 50,000, depending on insurance status (ZPZR). TRAP: the intervention act ZIURS, which some guides report as already in force with higher limits, is subject to a subsequent legislative referendum. FURS states (16 Oct 2026) that ZPZR still applies for entry and exit. If ZIURS fails, taxpayers who do not meet ZPZR conditions will be moved to actual-expense taxation for all of 2026, with full bookkeeping.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw in local currency'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
